title: Martial 10.47: the poem and this translation
greek: Vitam quae faciant beatiorem, / iucundissime Martialis, haec sunt
short: A list of what makes life happy, addressed to Martial's namesake friend Julius Martialis; here in Robert Fletcher's couplets of 1656.
body: Epigram 10.47 is addressed to Julius Martialis, Martial's closest friend, whose villa on the Janiculum he praises in 4.64 and to whom he writes in 1.15 and 5.20. The Latin is thirteen Phalaecean hendecasyllables: a list of nouns describing the happy life, ending with three wishes. Paley and Stone called it an epigram 'of the highest merit' in both form and matter. Post suggests Martial may have been answering a theme set by his friend. The archive gives the version by R. Fletcher in Ex Otio Negotium (1656), in rhymed octosyllabic couplets with seventeenth-century spelling ('happyer', 'plainesse', 'kinde'). Line references follow Fletcher's lines.

title: 'the happyer life': a philosophical topic
short: Beata vita, 'the happy life', was the subject of philosophical treatises; Martial gives a practical, unsystematic answer.
body: Beatior vita ('a happier life') recalls the philosophers' question about the beata vita, discussed by Cicero (Tusculan Disputations 5) and Seneca (De Vita Beata). Martial's answer borrows from both Epicurean and Stoic ideals: modest independence, a quiet mind, friends and no fear of death. But it is presented as a list of comforts rather than an argument. It was among the earliest of Martial's epigrams to be rendered into English, notably by Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey ('Martial, the things for to attain / The happy life be these, I find'), printed in Tottel's Miscellany (1557). Fletcher adds 'and day', which has no Latin equivalent and is there for the rhyme.

anchor: Means not sweat for, but resign'd
title: 'Means not sweat for, but resign'd'
greek: res non parta labore, sed relicta
short: Wealth 'not earned by toil but left to one': inherited money; 'resign'd' here means handed over or bequeathed.
body: The Latin is res non parta labore, sed relicta, 'property not won by labour but left (by inheritance)'. Post glosses res as money or estate, and relicta as 'inherited', from kinsfolk or friends. He cites Plato's Republic (330 B-C), where Socrates observes that those who inherit wealth care less for it than those who have made it. Paley and Stone give the same explanation: self-made men overvalue money and do not enjoy it. Fletcher's 'Means' is apt. 'Resign'd' uses resign in its old sense of 'to hand over, surrender to another' (OED, resign v.), which turns the bequest into a gift.

title: 'Fire without end'
short: An ever-burning hearth: a household always supplied with fuel and food.
body: The Latin focus perennis means 'a hearth that lasts all year'. Paley and Stone explain it as a hearth well supplied throughout the year, either with fuel or with food, as we speak of keeping the kitchen fire going. Post calls it a metonymy for an unfailing supply of food and of the fuel to cook it, and compares Tibullus 1.1.5-6, where the poet wishes for a modest life with a hearth always alight. Fletcher's 'Fire without end' is literal and slightly grand, but it keeps the image of the burning hearth.

title: 'fields still in kinde'
short: Latin: 'a farm not ungrateful', one that repays the work spent on it. Fletcher's 'still in kinde' means always true to their nature, or always yielding.
body: The Latin is non ingratus ager, 'a not ungrateful field', that is, land that gives a good return. Post compares Cicero, On Old Age 51, on the earth that never refuses command and always repays with interest what it receives. Fletcher's phrase 'still in kinde' is harder. 'Still' means 'always' in older English. 'In kind' probably means 'according to their nature' (kind = nature), so that the fields keep producing as fields should. It could also mean 'in produce', the OED's sense of payment in goods rather than money. 'Kinde' is Fletcher's spelling.

title: 'No strife, no office'
short: No lawsuits and seldom the toga: freedom from litigation and from the formal duties of public and client life.
body: The Latin is lis numquam, toga rara, mens quieta, 'never a lawsuit, the toga rarely, a quiet mind'. Post glosses lis as lawsuits and notes that the toga was costly, hot and heavy. It had to be worn at the games and, by clients, when they attended their patrons each morning. Martial often complains of the client's toga and praises the country, where it is not needed. Paley and Stone explain toga rara as the toga seldom required, in serving a patron or appearing in the forum. Fletcher replaces the garment with what it stood for: 'no office', no public duty.

title: 'inward peace'
short: A quiet mind, free from anxiety: the tranquillity that Epicureans called ataraxia.
body: Mens quieta, 'a quiet mind', is glossed by Post simply as 'free from worry'. The phrase recalls the philosophical goal of tranquillity, ataraxia in Epicurean terms or tranquillitas animi in Seneca's essay of that name. In Martial's list it comes after the removal of external troubles, lawsuits and duties, as though peace of mind followed from them. Fletcher's 'inward peace' is close, and it gives the phrase a slightly devotional colour, perhaps natural to an English poet writing in the 1650s, soon after the Civil War.

anchor: Free strength, a body sans disease
title: 'Free strength, a body sans disease'
short: Vires ingenuae, the strength proper to a free gentleman, and a healthy body; the Latin line is a chiasmus.
body: The Latin is vires ingenuae, salubre corpus, 'free-born strength, a healthy body'. Post explains vires ingenuae as the strength a gentleman needs, not the brute force of a labourer, or possibly 'innate' strength. Paley and Stone render it 'constitutional strength'. Post notes the chiasmus (noun-adjective, adjective-noun) and compares Juvenal's mens sana in corpore sano (10.356). Fletcher's 'Free strength' keeps the social sense of ingenuus ('free-born'), and 'sans' is the French-derived word for 'without', common in English poetry (OED, sans prep.).

title: 'A prudent plainesse'
short: Frankness tempered by tact: openness of character that does not give offence.
body: The Latin prudens simplicitas means 'prudent simplicity', or as Paley and Stone put it, openness of character too discreet to give offence by telling unwelcome truths. Post compares Martial's praise of Romana simplicitas (11.20.10) and a 'simple' honest friend in 1.39. The phrase is almost an oxymoron, since simplicitas is guileless and prudens calculating. Fletcher's 'plainesse' (plainness) keeps the idea of plain dealing, and 'prudent' is the cognate of prudens.

title: 'equal friends'
short: Pares, 'equal' or 'well-matched': friends of one's own standing, or congenial companions.
body: The Latin pares amici may mean friends equal in rank and wealth, on the ancient principle that true friendship exists only between equals. Or, as Post and Paley and Stone prefer, it may mean well-matched, congenial friends. Post cites Cicero's proverb that like readily gathers with like (On Old Age 7) and Horace's dinner invitation in Epistles 1.5, where he will see to it that equal is joined with equal. Fletcher's 'equal friends' keeps the ambiguity. Martial knew the alternative well: much of his work satirises the unequal friendship of patron and client.

title: 'Cheap Cates, not scraped from the world's ends'
short: Plain food, not luxuries gathered from distant lands; 'cates' is an old word for delicacies or provisions.
body: The Latin is convictus facilis, sine arte mensa, 'easy company, a table without art'. Post explains this as a plain, old-fashioned dinner, plainly served, like the one Martial describes in the next epigram (10.48). Paley and Stone add that sine arte means without the elaborate creations of artistic cooks. Fletcher omits convictus facilis (good-natured guests) and expands the plain table. 'Cates' are choice foods or provisions (OED, cate n.). 'Not scraped from the world's ends' turns the absence of art into an attack on imported luxuries. That attack is a theme elsewhere in Martial and in Roman satire, but it is Fletcher's addition here.

title: 'A night not drown'd, but free from care'
greek: nox non ebria, sed soluta curis
short: A night not drunk but 'released from cares': enough wine to forget troubles, not so much as to be drunk.
body: The Latin is nox non ebria, sed soluta curis, 'a night not drunken, but loosed from cares'. Post reads this as just enough wine at the after-dinner drinking (comissatio) to forget the burdens of life. Paley and Stone say the cares are relieved by the social cup, not drowned in drink, quoting Propertius on drinking till dawn. Fletcher's 'not drown'd' supplies an image of drowning in wine where the Latin says simply 'not drunken'. 'Free from care' renders soluta curis well.

title: 'Sheets never sad, and yet chast are'
greek: non tristis torus, et tamen pudicus
short: A marriage-bed not gloomy or prudish, yet chaste; 'sad' in Fletcher's English means grave or sober.
body: The Latin is non tristis torus, et tamen pudicus, 'a bed not severe, and yet chaste'. Torus ('couch') stands for the marriage-bed, and so for a wife. Paley and Stone gloss it as 'a wife who is virtuous without being a prude', and Post glosses tristis as 'prudish'. Ker's prose translation in the archive (martial/1210) also speaks of a wife. Fletcher keeps the bed ('Sheets') rather than the wife. His 'sad' is used in its older sense of 'serious, grave, sober' (OED, sad adj.), a good match for tristis. 'Chast' is his spelling of 'chaste'.

anchor: makes short the shades of night
title: 'Sleep that makes short the shades of night'
short: Sleep so sound that the dark hours seem brief.
body: The Latin is somnus, qui faciat breves tenebras, 'sleep that makes the darkness short'. Paley and Stone explain it as a sleep so sound that the dark hours seem to pass quickly. Post calls it sound, unbroken sleep, the opposite of the sleepless nights Martial describes elsewhere, such as the noise of Rome in 12.57. The line closes the list of physical comforts. Fletcher's 'shades of night' is a poetic periphrasis for tenebras ('darkness').

title: 'Art such thou would'st be, if there might / A choice be offer'd'
greek: quod sis esse velis nihilque malis
short: 'Be willing to be what you are, and prefer nothing else': contentment with one's lot. Fletcher turns it into a statement.
body: The Latin is quod sis esse velis nihilque malis, 'wish to be what you are, and prefer nothing'. Post notes the abrupt change from the list of nouns to subjunctives of wish. He argues that a list of the essentials of happiness is really a prayer for them, and compares Juvenal 10.356-62. Paley and Stone render 'to be willing to be what you are, and to prefer no other lot'. Fletcher turns the wish into a description: you already are what you would choose to be if you were offered a choice. The meaning is close, but he loses the imperative force. His syntax ('Art such thou would'st be') is compressed and needs careful reading.

title: 'nor dost fear / Nor wish thy last dayes exit here'
greek: summum nec metuas diem nec optes
short: Neither fear nor long for your last day: the classic philosophical attitude to death, balanced in a single line.
body: The last line, summum nec metuas diem nec optes, 'neither fear your final day nor wish for it', is the poem's most quoted. Neither fearing death (the Epicurean lesson) nor longing for it (as a release from misery) is the balanced attitude of the sage. Paley and Stone explain nec optes with reference to tormenting diseases that might make a man wish for death. Fletcher's 'thy last dayes exit here' adds 'here', suggesting departure from this world. Surrey's version ends with the parallel advice to neither wish nor fear death.
